title: Grade 11 Mathematics — Introduction to 3D Geometry + Limits
description: 3D coordinates, distance formula, section formula, midpoint (CBSE Ch. 12) + introduction to limits (Ch. 13)
subject: mathematics

questions.question: A point in three-dimensional space is located by coordinates:
options: (x, y) — two values along two axes
(x, y, z) — three values along three mutually perpendicular axes
(x, y, z, t) — four values including time
questions.explanation: In 3D coordinate geometry, every point is represented by an ordered triple (x, y, z) measured along the three mutually perpendicular axes: x-axis, y-axis, and z-axis. These axes meet at the origin O(0, 0, 0).

questions.question: Three-dimensional space is divided into how many octants?
questions.explanation: Three coordinate planes (xy, yz, xz) divide 3D space into 8 octants (analogous to 4 quadrants in 2D). Each octant is defined by a specific combination of signs (+/−) for x, y, and z.

questions.question: A point lying on the x-axis has coordinates of the form:
questions.explanation: Any point on the x-axis has y = 0 and z = 0 (it lies on neither the y-axis nor the z-axis). So it is of the form (x, 0, 0) — only the x-coordinate varies.

questions.question: The distance from the origin O(0, 0, 0) to a point P(x, y, z) is:
questions.explanation: By the 3D extension of the Pythagorean theorem, OP = √(x² + y² + z²). This is the distance formula from the origin to any point in 3D space.

questions.question: The distance between points A(x₁, y₁, z₁) and B(x₂, y₂, z₂) in 3D space is:
questions.explanation: AB = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²]. This is the direct 3D generalisation of the 2D distance formula, using differences in all three coordinates.

questions.question: The midpoint of the line segment joining A(2, 4, −6) and B(4, −2, 6) is:
The distance between points P(1, 2, 3) and Q(4, 6, 3) is:
A point lies on the xy-plane. Which of its coordinates is zero?
questions.explanation: The xy-plane is defined by z = 0. Any point on the xy-plane has the form (x, y, 0) — its z-coordinate is zero. Similarly, points on the yz-plane have x = 0, and on the xz-plane have y = 0.

questions.question: Point R divides the segment joining A(1, 2, 3) and B(7, 8, 9) internally in the ratio 1:2. The coordinates of R are:
The midpoint M of AB is known as M = (3, 5, 7), and A = (1, 3, 5). Find B.
In calculus, the limit lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Factor: x² − 4 = (x−2)(x+2). For x ≠ 2, (x²−4)/(x−2) = x + 2. As x → 2, the limit = 2 + 2 = 4. Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factoring is required.

questions.question: The standard result lim(x→0) (sin x)/x equals:
questions.explanation: This is a fundamental trigonometric limit: lim(x→0) (sin x)/x = 1 (where x is in radians). Direct substitution gives 0/0 — but using the squeeze theorem or L'Hôpital's rule gives 1.

questions.question: A limit exists at a point x = a if and only if:
options: The function value f(a) is defined
The left-hand limit and right-hand limit are both equal
The derivative exists at x = a
questions.explanation: lim(x→a) f(x) exists if and only if the left-hand limit (LHL) = right-hand limit (RHL). The actual function value f(a) may not even be defined — limits describe the function's behaviour as x approaches a, not at a.

questions.question: lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x equals:
questions.explanation: Using the standard result: lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0. This follows because (1 − cos x)/x = (2sin²(x/2))/x → 2 · (x/2)/x · sin(x/2)/(x/2) → 0 as x → 0. Alternatively, L'Hôpital: sin x / 1 → 0.

questions.question: lim(x→∞) 1/x equals:
questions.explanation: As x grows without bound (x → ∞), 1/x becomes smaller and smaller, approaching 0. lim(x→∞) 1/x = 0. This is a fundamental result used in convergence of sequences and series.
